What makes a toad so amazing?

The bumpy-skinned toad is a relative of the frog, but it's an amphibian that does well even on drier ground. In old Korean folktales, it was also loved as an animal that brings good fortune.

content.alt: Toad - Nature and science facts about toads
content.text:
Nature and science facts about toads

A toad's skin is thicker, drier, and bumpier than a frog's, so it does well even on land a little way from water. The bumps on its back aren't warts but a skin structure that protects its body, and the saying "touching one gives you warts" is an old myth, not true. With its long tongue it eats pests like mosquitoes and bugs, which is helpful to people, and it lays its eggs in water and grows through metamorphosis by way of the tadpole stage.

Parent guide — how to nurture curiosity

Compare photos of a frog and a toad and look for differences in skin and habitat. Let your child know that "touching a toad won't give you warts (it's a myth)," and talk about how it helps by eating pests.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. Does touching a toad give you warts?
A. No. The bumps on its back are just a skin structure that protects its body — "getting warts" is an old myth, not true.

Q. How is a toad different from a frog?
A. A toad's skin is thicker, drier, and bumpier, so it does well even on land a little way from water.

Q. How can we observe toads at home?
A. Compare skin and habitat with a frog, and talk about how it helps by eating pests.
